trap.title: Department, office, or agency?
trap.body: This department is a big umbrella, and many of its parts have their own answer lines: the TSA, FEMA, the Coast Guard, and the Secret Service. A clue about airport screening or disaster relief might want that agency, not the whole department. It is also easy to mix it up with the FBI (part of the Justice Department), the CIA (an independent agency), or the White House office Tom Ridge led before the department existed.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this department” or “this cabinet department” wants Homeland Security, while “this agency” or “this branch” wants the part being described. Clues about a 2002 law, 22 agencies combined, or the first secretary, Tom Ridge, point to the department.
trap.line: Real answer line: Department of Homeland Security (or DHS; accept Homeland Security)

topics.name: Dust Bowl
topics.kicker: 1930s dust storms on the southern Plains · Drove “Okies” west to California
topics.briefing: During the 1930s, years of drought turned the over-plowed farmland of the southern Great Plains into the “Dust Bowl.” Winds whipped the bare soil into “black blizzards” that buried fences, darkened the sky at noon, and carried dust all the way to the East Coast. Hundreds of thousands of people, many mocked as “Okies,” headed west to California, a journey told in John Steinbeck’s novel _The Grapes of Wrath_.
topics.answerHtml: Dust Bowl (prompt on dust storms or black blizzards; do not accept “Great Depression”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The Associated Press reporter Robert Geiger is credited with naming this disaster in a story he wrote the day after Black Sunday. On that day, April 14, 1935, a giant wall of dust rolled across the panhandles of Oklahoma and Texas and turned the afternoon sky black.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1930s disaster in which drought and wind stripped soil from the southern Great Plains.

tossups.p: Hugh Hammond Bennett, known as the father of soil conservation, was testifying before a congressional committee in 1935 when a dust cloud from this disaster reportedly darkened the sky over Washington, D.C. That year, Bennett became the first chief of the new Soil Conservation Service.
tossups.r: That agency fought the soil erosion behind this disaster. For 10 points, name this disaster of the 1930s on the southern Great Plains.

tossups.p: The federal government’s Shelterbelt Project planted more than 200 million trees in rows stretching from North Dakota to Texas to slow the winds that worsened this disaster. Farmers were also paid to use contour plowing and to plant cover crops that held the soil in place.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1930s ecological disaster that drove many families off their farms on the Great Plains.

tossups.p: In a novel set during this disaster, a turtle slowly crosses a highway in one short chapter, and in another, tractors knock down tenant farmers’ houses. That novel calls Route 66 “the mother road, the road of flight.”
tossups.r: The novel, John Steinbeck’s _The Grapes of Wrath_, follows a family forced off its Oklahoma farm. For 10 points, name this 1930s disaster on the Great Plains.

tossups.p: In the song “Do Re Mi,” a folk singer warned people fleeing this disaster that California was a “garden of Eden” only for those who had money. That singer, who lived in Pampa, Texas, during this disaster, also wrote “So Long, It’s Been Good to Know Yuh” after a giant dust storm.
tossups.r: That singer, Woody Guthrie, also wrote “This Land Is Your Land.” For 10 points, name this disaster of the 1930s.

tossups.p: Arthur Rothstein’s 1936 photograph of a farmer and his two sons walking through a dust storm in Cimarron County, Oklahoma, became one of the best-known images of this disaster. Dorothea Lange also photographed families fleeing this disaster for a federal agency.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disaster in which drought and wind blew away the topsoil of the southern Plains in the 1930s.

tossups.p: High wheat prices during World War I led farmers on the southern Plains to plow up millions of acres of native grassland, in what historians call the “Great Plow-Up.” When a long drought hit in the 1930s, nothing was left to hold the dry soil in place.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disaster that followed, when huge dust storms swept across the farms of the southern Great Plains.

tossups.p: Karen Hesse’s Newbery Medal–winning novel _Out of the Dust_ tells, in free-verse poems, the story of Billie Jo, a girl whose family farms in the Oklahoma Panhandle during this disaster. Billie Jo dreams of leaving as dust storms bury her family’s fields.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disaster of the 1930s, when drought and wind turned Great Plains farmland to dust.

tossups.p: Pare Lorentz’s 1936 government documentary _The Plow That Broke the Plains_ showed how farming practices helped cause this disaster. Decades later, Ken Burns made a two-part documentary about this disaster, featuring interviews with people who had lived through it as children.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disaster of the 1930s, when “black blizzards” of dust swept the southern Great Plains.

tossups.p: In May 1934, a storm from this disaster carried dust all the way to Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C., and even onto ships in the Atlantic Ocean. Many people living through this disaster developed “dust pneumonia” from breathing in fine dirt.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1930s disaster, which was worst in the panhandles of Oklahoma and Texas.

tossups.p: In 1936, the Los Angeles police chief sent officers to California’s borders to turn back poor migrants in what critics called the “bum blockade.” Five years later, in _Edwards v. California_, the Supreme Court struck down a law that made it a crime to bring poor people into that state.
tossups.r: Many of those migrants were fleeing this disaster and were insulted as “Okies.” For 10 points, name this 1930s disaster on the Great Plains.

tossups.p: During this disaster, some drivers dragged chains behind their cars to ground the static electricity built up by swirling dust, and families stuffed wet rags around their windows to keep the dirt out. The worst storms, called “black blizzards,” could turn noon as dark as night.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disaster of drought and dust storms that struck the southern Great Plains in the 1930s.

tossups.p: In 1934, the federal Drought Relief Service bought cattle from ranchers who could no longer feed them during this disaster. Two years later, a new law paid farmers to plant grasses and legumes instead of wheat to keep the soil from blowing away.
tossups.r: Both were part of Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal. For 10 points, name this 1930s disaster on the Great Plains.

tossups.p: Timothy Egan’s National Book Award–winning history _The Worst Hard Time_ tells the stories of families who stayed on the southern Plains through this disaster instead of leaving. Egan describes towns like Boise City, Oklahoma, and Dalhart, Texas, buried in drifting dirt.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disaster of the 1930s caused by drought, wind, and over-plowing.

tossups.p: Many families fleeing this disaster stayed at government camps for farmworkers in California, such as the Arvin camp, nicknamed “Weedpatch.” A novelist who visited that camp dedicated his book about these migrants partly to its manager, Tom Collins, “who lived it.”
tossups.r: That novelist was John Steinbeck. For 10 points, name this 1930s disaster that drove thousands of “Okies” to California.

clues.t: Disaster of the 1930s: drought and strong winds blew away the topsoil of the southern Great Plains
Setting of John Steinbeck’s _The Grapes of Wrath_ (1939), about the Joad family’s trip from Oklahoma to California
Hundreds of thousands of migrants, insulted as “Okies,” moved west to California looking for work
Struck during the Great Depression; Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal tried to help farmers recover
“Black Sunday” (April 14, 1935): a giant dust storm swept across the southern Plains
Caused by drought plus over-plowing: farmers had torn up the native grasses that held the soil (the “Great Plow-Up”)
Worst in the panhandles of Oklahoma and Texas, plus parts of Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico
Huge dust storms called “black blizzards” could turn noon as dark as night
Hugh Hammond Bennett led the new Soil Conservation Service (1935) to fight soil erosion
Shelterbelt Project: more than 200 million trees planted in rows from North Dakota to Texas to break the wind
Farmers learned contour plowing and planted cover crops to hold the soil in place
Folk singer Woody Guthrie, who lived in Pampa, Texas, wrote songs about it, like “Do Re Mi” and “So Long, It’s Been Good to Know Yuh”
Dorothea Lange photographed migrant families for the federal government
Migrants drove west on Route 66, which _The Grapes of Wrath_ calls “the mother road”
Associated Press reporter Robert Geiger is credited with naming it in a story the day after Black Sunday
Bennett was testifying before a congressional committee in 1935 when a dust cloud reportedly darkened the sky over Washington, D.C.
A May 1934 storm carried dust to Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C., and onto ships in the Atlantic
Many people got “dust pneumonia” from breathing fine dirt; drivers dragged chains to ground static electricity
Arthur Rothstein’s 1936 photo shows a farmer and two sons walking through a dust storm in Cimarron County, Oklahoma
Pare Lorentz’s government documentary _The Plow That Broke the Plains_ (1936); Ken Burns made a documentary about it in 2012
Karen Hesse’s Newbery-winning _Out of the Dust_ tells Billie Jo’s story in free-verse poems
Timothy Egan’s _The Worst Hard Time_ (National Book Award) tells of families who stayed on the Plains
_Edwards v. California_ (1941) struck down a law against bringing poor migrants into California; Los Angeles police ran a “bum blockade” in 1936
The Drought Relief Service bought ranchers’ starving cattle (1934); a 1936 law paid farmers to plant grasses and legumes instead of wheat
Many migrants stayed at government camps like Arvin (“Weedpatch”); Steinbeck dedicated his novel partly to its manager, Tom Collins
A turtle slowly crossing a highway fills one short chapter of _The Grapes of Wrath_

trap.title: Dust Bowl or Depression?
trap.body: The Dust Bowl happened during the Great Depression, so the two share clues like Franklin Roosevelt, the New Deal, Dorothea Lange’s photographs, and _The Grapes of Wrath_. Real answer lines treat them as different answers: the Great Depression was a nationwide economic crisis that began with the 1929 stock market crash, while the Dust Bowl was an environmental disaster on the southern Plains. Saying “Great Depression” on a Dust Bowl tossup is wrong.
trap.fix: Listen for weather and land: drought, dust storms, “black blizzards,” Black Sunday, plowed-up grassland, soil conservation, shelterbelts, and the Oklahoma or Texas panhandles mean the Dust Bowl. Failing banks, unemployment, breadlines, and the stock market crash mean the Great Depression.
trap.line: Real answer line: Dust Bowl (prompt on dust storms; do not accept “Great Depression”)

topics.name: Election of 1992
topics.kicker: Clinton beats Bush and Perot · Famous for “It’s the economy, stupid”
topics.briefing: After the 1991 Gulf War, President George H. W. Bush had approval ratings near 90 percent, but a recession and his broken promise of “no new taxes” became major issues by election time. Arkansas governor Bill Clinton, whose campaign’s motto was “It’s the economy, stupid,” won the presidency, while Texas businessman Ross Perot won about 19 percent of the popular vote, the best showing by a candidate outside the two major parties since 1912.
topics.answerHtml: Election of 1992 (or 1992 presidential election; prompt on presidential election; do not accept other years)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The documentary _The War Room_ followed the strategists James Carville and George Stephanopoulos through this campaign. Carville hung a sign in the campaign’s Little Rock headquarters listing three reminders: “Change vs. more of the same,” “Don’t forget health care,” and a line about the economy.
tossups.r: That line became famous as “It’s the economy, stupid.” For 10 points, name this election in which Bill Clinton defeated George H. W. Bush.

tossups.p: Pat Buchanan challenged the sitting president in the Republican primaries during this campaign, attacking him for breaking his 1988 pledge, “Read my lips: no new taxes.” That president had agreed to a 1990 budget deal that raised some taxes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election in which George H. W. Bush lost his bid for a second term to Bill Clinton.

tossups.p: Former California governor Jerry Brown ran in the Democratic primaries during this campaign, accepting donations of no more than $100. Another candidate in those primaries called himself “the Comeback Kid” after finishing second to Paul Tsongas [“SONG-gus”] in New Hampshire.
tossups.r: That “Comeback Kid,” Arkansas governor Bill Clinton, won the nomination. For 10 points, name this presidential election.

tossups.p: One candidate in this election announced on _Larry King Live_ that he would run if volunteers got his name on the ballot in all 50 states. That candidate dropped out in July, returned in October, and spent millions of his own dollars on half-hour TV programs filled with charts.
tossups.r: That Texas businessman, Ross Perot, won about 19 percent of the popular vote. For 10 points, name this election.

tossups.p: This election featured the first presidential debate held in a “town hall” style, at the University of Richmond, where the sitting president was criticized for glancing at his watch. Its debates were also the first to put three presidential candidates on the same stage.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election in which Bill Clinton, George H. W. Bush, and Ross Perot debated.

tossups.p: Wearing sunglasses, one candidate in this election played “Heartbreak Hotel” on the saxophone on _The Arsenio Hall Show_. That candidate’s campaign song was Fleetwood Mac’s “Don’t Stop,” which urged listeners to keep “thinking about tomorrow.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election won by that saxophone-playing Arkansas governor, Bill Clinton, over George H. W. Bush.

tossups.p: Carol Moseley Braun of Illinois became the first Black woman elected to the U.S. Senate in this election, which was nicknamed the “Year of the Woman.” California also elected two women, Dianne Feinstein and Barbara Boxer, to the Senate on the same day.
tossups.r: At the top of the ticket, Bill Clinton won the presidency. For 10 points, name this election.

tossups.p: During this campaign, an independent candidate warned of a “giant sucking sound” of American jobs moving to Mexico if a planned trade deal was approved. That candidate’s running mate was James Stockdale, a retired admiral who had been a prisoner of war in Vietnam.
tossups.r: That candidate, Ross Perot, won no electoral votes. For 10 points, name this election won by Bill Clinton.

tossups.p: After the Gulf War in 1991, the sitting president’s approval rating soared to nearly 90 percent, but it fell sharply during a recession before this election. His opponent’s campaign focused on the weak economy and on health care.
tossups.r: That president, George H. W. Bush, lost to Bill Clinton. For 10 points, name this election.

tossups.p: The winning ticket in this election was the first in which both candidates had been born after World War II, as members of the baby boom generation. Both men were Southerners: one was the governor of Arkansas, and the other was a senator from Tennessee.
tossups.r: Those men were Bill Clinton and Al Gore, who defeated George H. W. Bush and Dan Quayle. For 10 points, name this election.

tossups.p: At their convention in New York City’s Madison Square Garden during this campaign, Democrats showed a short film called _The Man from Hope_, about their nominee’s childhood in a small Arkansas town. Republicans held their convention in Houston’s Astrodome.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election, after which Bill Clinton became the 42nd president.

tossups.p: The winner of this election had chaired the Democratic Leadership Council, a group of “New Democrats” who wanted their party to move toward the political center. He became the first Democrat to win the presidency since Jimmy Carter.
tossups.r: He received 370 electoral votes but only about 43 percent of the popular vote. For 10 points, name this election won by Bill Clinton.

tossups.p: One candidate in this election had founded the computer company Electronic Data Systems, and he later started the Reform Party and ran again four years later. In this election, he won the best share of the vote for a candidate outside the two major parties since Theodore Roosevelt in 1912.
tossups.r: That candidate was Ross Perot. For 10 points, name this election in which Bill Clinton beat George H. W. Bush.

tossups.p: In this election, the Democratic ticket carried California for the first time since 1964 and won a total of 32 states plus Washington, D.C. Its vice-presidential candidate debated the sitting vice president and a retired admiral.
tossups.r: That Democratic running mate was Al Gore. For 10 points, name this election in which Bill Clinton defeated George H. W. Bush.

tossups.p: Secretary of State James Baker left his post in August to take charge of the sitting president’s reelection effort during this campaign. That president, who had led the country through the Gulf War, won only 168 electoral votes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election in which George H. W. Bush lost to Bill Clinton.

clues.t: Democrat Bill Clinton defeated the sitting Republican president, George H. W. Bush
Independent Ross Perot, a Texas businessman, won about 19 percent of the popular vote but no electoral votes
The Clinton campaign’s famous motto: “It’s the economy, stupid”
Running mates: Senator Al Gore of Tennessee (with Clinton) and Vice President Dan Quayle (with Bush)
Bush had broken his 1988 pledge, “Read my lips: no new taxes,” in a 1990 budget deal
Bush’s approval soared to nearly 90 percent after the Gulf War (1991), then fell during a recession
Clinton called himself “the Comeback Kid” after finishing second to Paul Tsongas in the New Hampshire primary
Perot announced on _Larry King Live_ that he would run if volunteers put him on the ballot in all 50 states; he quit in July and returned in October
First “town hall” presidential debate (University of Richmond), where Bush glanced at his watch; the first debates with three candidates
Clinton played “Heartbreak Hotel” on the saxophone on _The Arsenio Hall Show_
Clinton won 370 electoral votes and 32 states but only about 43 percent of the popular vote; Bush won 168
Pat Buchanan challenged Bush in the Republican primaries
Clinton was the first Democrat to win since Jimmy Carter; Bush was the first sitting president to lose reelection since Carter
James Carville’s sign in the Little Rock “war room” listed change, the economy, and health care; the documentary _The War Room_ followed him and George Stephanopoulos
Perot warned of a “giant sucking sound” of jobs moving to Mexico under a planned trade deal (NAFTA)
Perot’s running mate was retired admiral James Stockdale, a former prisoner of war in Vietnam
Perot, founder of Electronic Data Systems, spent millions of his own dollars on half-hour TV programs full of charts
Perot’s share was the best for a candidate outside the two major parties since Theodore Roosevelt (1912); he later founded the Reform Party and ran again in 1996
“Year of the Woman”: Carol Moseley Braun became the first Black woman elected to the Senate; California elected Dianne Feinstein and Barbara Boxer
Democrats met at Madison Square Garden and showed the film _The Man from Hope_; Republicans met in Houston’s Astrodome
Clinton and Gore were the first winning ticket of two baby boomers, both Southerners (Arkansas and Tennessee)
Clinton had chaired the Democratic Leadership Council, a group of centrist “New Democrats”
Former California governor Jerry Brown ran in the Democratic primaries, taking donations of no more than $100
Clinton’s campaign song was Fleetwood Mac’s “Don’t Stop” (“thinking about tomorrow”)
Clinton carried California, the first Democrat to win it since 1964
Secretary of State James Baker resigned in August to run Bush’s reelection effort

trap.title: Name the year
trap.body: Election tossups describe the candidates but want the year, so you must connect the people to the right race. George H. W. Bush won in 1988 and lost here; Bill Clinton won here and again in 1996, when Ross Perot ran a second time with much less support. Answering “Bill Clinton” or “Ross Perot” is wrong when the question asks for the election.
trap.fix: Anchor the year with its clues: “It’s the economy, stupid,” the Comeback Kid, the town-hall debate, Perot’s charts and “giant sucking sound,” and the Year of the Woman all mean 1992. Bob Dole as the Republican nominee means 1996. Say “the election of 1992” or just “1992.”
trap.line: Real answer line: United States presidential election of 1992 (prompt on presidential election)

topics.name: Election of 2000
topics.kicker: Bush beats Gore by 537 Florida votes · Recount ended by the Supreme Court
topics.briefing: The 2000 presidential race between Texas governor George W. Bush and Vice President Al Gore came down to Florida, where the vote was so close that it led to weeks of recounts and lawsuits over “butterfly ballots” and “hanging chads.” On December 12, the Supreme Court’s ruling in _Bush v. Gore_ ended the recount, leaving Bush ahead by 537 votes. Gore won the national popular vote but lost in the Electoral College, 271 to 266.
topics.answerHtml: Election of 2000 (or 2000 presidential election; prompt on presidential election or Florida recount; do not accept “Bush v. Gore”)
reject: bush v palm beach county canvassing board

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The Supreme Court ruled 7–2 that Florida’s recount in this election, which used different standards in different counties, violated the Equal Protection Clause. By a 5–4 vote, the justices also ruled that there was no time left for a new recount.
tossups.r: That December ruling, in _Bush v. Gore_, ended the recount. For 10 points, name this presidential election.

tossups.p: Theresa LePore, the elections supervisor of Palm Beach County, designed a “butterfly ballot” for this election that listed candidates on two facing pages, with one column of punch holes down the middle. Some voters said that ballot led them to vote for Pat Buchanan by mistake.
tossups.r: Recount workers later examined punch-card ballots for “hanging” chads. For 10 points, name this election in which George W. Bush defeated Al Gore.

tossups.p: Florida’s secretary of state, Katherine Harris, certified one candidate as the winner of her state in this election by just 537 votes. That candidate’s lead after the first count on election night had been fewer than 2,000 votes.
tossups.r: Weeks of recounts and lawsuits followed. For 10 points, name this election in which George W. Bush defeated Al Gore.

tossups.p: Ralph Nader won more than 97,000 votes in Florida as the Green Party’s candidate in this election, while Pat Buchanan ran on the Reform Party ticket. Nationwide, Nader won almost 3 percent of the popular vote.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election decided by a few hundred votes in Florida, in which George W. Bush beat Al Gore.

tossups.p: In this election, Senator Joe Lieberman of Connecticut became the first Jewish candidate on a major party’s presidential ticket. His opponent for vice president, Dick Cheney, had led the search for a running mate before being chosen himself.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election in which Lieberman’s running mate, Al Gore, lost to George W. Bush.

tossups.p: One elector from Washington, D.C., left her ballot blank after this election to protest the city’s lack of voting representation in Congress, so the winner’s final margin in the Electoral College was 271 votes to 266.
tossups.r: The loser won the national popular vote by more than half a million votes. For 10 points, name this election in which Al Gore lost to George W. Bush.

tossups.p: On election night, TV networks projected that one candidate had won Florida, took it back, and later declared that his opponent had won the state. The first candidate then phoned his opponent to concede, only to call back later that night and take back his concession.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election that ended weeks later when Al Gore conceded to George W. Bush.

tossups.p: One candidate in this election lost his home state of Tennessee, whose 11 electoral votes would have given him the presidency. That candidate, the sitting vice president, also lost Arkansas, the home state of the president he served under.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election in which Al Gore lost to George W. Bush.

tossups.p: In this election, Hillary Clinton became the first First Lady elected to public office, winning a Senate seat from New York. Voters also chose a president who was the son of a former president, the first since John Quincy Adams.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election in which George W. Bush defeated Al Gore.

tossups.p: During the legal fight after this election, former secretaries of state James Baker and Warren Christopher led the opposing campaigns’ teams. At the Supreme Court, Theodore Olson argued for one candidate and David Boies [“BOYZ”] argued for the other.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election decided by a Florida recount, in which George W. Bush beat Al Gore.

tossups.p: Problems with punch-card voting machines in this election led Congress to pass the Help America Vote Act in 2002, which gave states money to buy new voting equipment and created the Election Assistance Commission.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election decided by a recount in Florida, which George W. Bush won over Al Gore.

tossups.p: One candidate in this election described his philosophy as “compassionate conservatism,” while the other promised to protect Social Security money in a “lockbox.” The first candidate was the governor of Texas, and the second was the sitting vice president.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election in which George W. Bush defeated Al Gore.

tossups.p: Before the final ruling in this election’s legal fight, the U.S. Supreme Court unanimously sent back a Florida decision in _Bush v. Palm Beach County Canvassing Board_. On December 8, the Florida Supreme Court ordered a statewide hand recount of ballots with no machine-recorded vote for president.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election in which a recount in Florida decided whether George W. Bush or Al Gore won.

tossups.p: One candidate in this election conceded in a televised speech on December 13, saying that he strongly disagreed with the Supreme Court’s decision but accepted it. That candidate had served eight years as vice president under Bill Clinton.
tossups.r: The day before, the Court’s ruling had ended the Florida recount. For 10 points, name this election in which Al Gore lost to George W. Bush.

tossups.p: This was the first election since 1888 in which the winner of the national popular vote lost the presidency. Florida’s 25 electoral votes decided it, and the winning candidate’s younger brother Jeb was governor of Florida at the time.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election in which George W. Bush defeated Vice President Al Gore after weeks of recounts.

trap.title: Election or court case?
trap.body: This election’s most famous clues, the Florida recount, hanging chads, and the Supreme Court, also lead tossups whose answer is the case _Bush v. Gore_, and some questions ask for George W. Bush or Al Gore themselves. Answering “Bush v. Gore” when the question says “this election” is wrong, and so is naming the election when it asks for “this case.” The election of 1876, which also turned on disputed Florida votes, is a different answer.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this election” wants 2000, “this case” or “this ruling” wants _Bush v. Gore_, and “this candidate” wants a person. Rutherford B. Hayes, Samuel Tilden, and a fifteen-member commission mean 1876, not 2000.
trap.line: Real answer line: United States presidential election of 2000 (prompt on presidential election; do not accept “Bush v. Gore”)

topics.name: Electoral College
topics.kicker: How Americans choose a president · Takes 270 of 538 electoral votes
topics.briefing: When Americans vote for president, they are really choosing electors, who cast the official votes weeks later. The framers of the Constitution created this system in 1787 as a compromise between letting Congress pick the president and letting the people vote directly. Since 1964, there have been 538 electors, and a candidate needs 270 of their votes to win, so a candidate can win the most votes nationwide and still lose.
topics.answerHtml: Electoral College (prompt on electors or electoral votes; do not accept “popular vote”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In _Chiafalo v. Washington_, the Supreme Court ruled unanimously in 2020 that states may punish members of this body who break their pledge to vote for their party’s candidate. Seven of its members broke their pledges in 2016.
tossups.r: Such members are called “faithless electors.” For 10 points, name this body of 538 people that formally elects the president.

tossups.p: Under the original Constitution, each member of this body cast two votes for president, and the runner-up became vice president. After Thomas Jefferson and his running mate, Aaron Burr, tied in 1800, the Twelfth Amendment made members vote separately for president and vice president.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of electors, created by Article II of the Constitution, that chooses the president.

tossups.p: Alexander Hamilton defended this institution in _Federalist_ No. 68, arguing that a small group of people chosen for that one task should pick the president. The name most people use for this institution does not appear anywhere in the Constitution.
tossups.r: A candidate needs 270 of its 538 votes to win. For 10 points, name this body that formally elects the U.S. president.

tossups.p: Nebraska first split its votes in this system in 2008, when Barack Obama won the congressional district around Omaha. Nebraska and Maine are the only states that give some of their votes in this system to the winner of each congressional district.
tossups.r: Every other state gives all of its electors to the statewide winner. For 10 points, name this body that formally chooses the president.

tossups.p: Residents of Washington, D.C., could not vote for president until 1964. The Twenty-third Amendment, ratified in 1961, gave the city members in this body, but no more than the least populous state has.
tossups.r: Each state has as many members in it as it has senators and representatives combined. For 10 points, name this body that elects the president.

tossups.p: In 1837, the Senate picked the vice president for the only time, after no candidate for that office won a majority in this institution. The House of Representatives picks the president in that situation, as it did after the election of 1824, when it chose John Quincy Adams.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this institution in which a candidate needs 270 of 538 votes to become president.

tossups.p: Samuel Tilden in 1876 and Grover Cleveland in 1888 both won the most popular votes but lost the presidency because of this institution; in 1888, Benjamin Harrison won a majority of its votes instead.
tossups.r: The same thing happened to Al Gore in 2000 and Hillary Clinton in 2016. For 10 points, name this group of 538 electors that elects the president.

tossups.p: In 1820, James Monroe won every vote in this body except one, which William Plumer of New Hampshire cast for John Quincy Adams. The only president ever to win all of its votes did so in both 1789 and 1792.
tossups.r: That president was George Washington. For 10 points, name this body that formally elects the president.

tossups.p: After disputes over 20 votes from Florida, Louisiana, South Carolina, and Oregon in 1876, a fifteen-member commission awarded all of them to Rutherford B. Hayes, who won this body’s vote by one.
tossups.r: An 1887 law set rules for counting its votes. For 10 points, name this body of electors that formally chooses the president.

tossups.p: Members of this body meet in their own states in December to cast their votes. On January 6, the vice president, acting as President of the Senate, opens the certificates of those votes in a joint session of Congress, and the votes are counted.
tossups.r: A majority of its 538 votes elects the president. For 10 points, name this body.

tossups.p: After the 2020 census, Texas gained two votes in this institution and California lost one, because each state’s share changes as its population shifts. Even the least populous states have three votes in it.
tossups.r: A state’s number equals its senators plus its representatives. For 10 points, name this institution, in which a candidate needs 270 votes to win the presidency.

tossups.p: George Wallace won 46 votes in this body in 1968, and Strom Thurmond won 39 in 1948, both running outside the two major parties. Ross Perot won almost 19 percent of the popular vote in 1992 but none of this body’s votes.
tossups.r: A candidate needs 270 of its 538 votes. For 10 points, name this body that formally elects the president.

tossups.p: The Constitution lets each state legislature decide how to choose members of this body, and South Carolina’s legislature picked them itself, without a popular vote, through 1860. Members of Congress are not allowed to serve in this body.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this body of 538 electors that formally chooses the president and vice president.

tossups.p: States that join the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact agree to give all their votes in this body to whichever candidate wins the most votes nationwide. The compact takes effect only once states holding a majority of this body’s votes have joined.
tossups.r: That majority is 270 of 538. For 10 points, name this body that formally elects the president.

tossups.p: In 1984, Ronald Reagan won 525 votes in this body, the most ever, while Walter Mondale carried only his home state of Minnesota and Washington, D.C. Four years earlier, Reagan had won 489 of its votes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this body of 538 electors that formally elects the president and vice president.

In 1820, James Monroe won every vote but one, which William Plumer cast for John Quincy Adams

trap.title: Which body decides?
trap.body: Clues for this answer line mention several groups: the House picks the president if no one wins a majority, the Senate picks the vice president in that case, and Congress counts the votes on January 6. Those clues tempt players to answer “House of Representatives” or “Congress.” Clues about popular-vote losers like Al Gore can also tempt an answer of “popular vote” or a specific election.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this body,” “this institution,” or “this system” with 538 members, 270 votes to win, changes made by the 12th and 23rd Amendments, or “faithless” members, say “Electoral College.” Saying only “electors” earns a prompt, so be ready to give the full name.

topics.name: Ethan Allen
topics.kicker: Leader of the Green Mountain Boys · Seized Fort Ticonderoga in 1775
topics.briefing: Ethan Allen led the Green Mountain Boys, a frontier militia that fought New York’s claims to the land that became Vermont. In May 1775, just weeks after the Revolution began, he and Benedict Arnold surprised the British at Fort Ticonderoga in a dawn raid, and Allen later wrote that he demanded its surrender “in the name of the Great Jehovah and the Continental Congress.” Captured near Montreal that fall, he spent nearly three years as a prisoner.
topics.answerHtml: Ethan Allen (prompt on Allen; do not accept “Ira Allen” or “Benedict Arnold”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: At dawn on May 10, 1775, this man’s small force rushed into a lightly guarded fort, and Captain William Delaplace surrendered without a battle. This man later wrote that he had demanded the surrender “in the name of the Great Jehovah and the Continental Congress.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this leader of the Green Mountain Boys who captured Fort Ticonderoga with Benedict Arnold.

tossups.p: This man was shipped across the Atlantic in chains and held at Pendennis Castle in England. He had been captured in September 1775 during a failed attempt to seize Montreal, and he was finally freed in a prisoner exchange in 1778.
tossups.r: In May 1775, he had captured Fort Ticonderoga. For 10 points, name this leader of the Green Mountain Boys.

tossups.p: This man was exchanged for the British officer Archibald Campbell in 1778 after nearly three years as a prisoner of war. The next year, he published a popular _Narrative_ describing his harsh treatment on British ships and in British jails.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this patriot who had led the Green Mountain Boys in capturing Fort Ticonderoga.

tossups.p: This man’s 1784 book _Reason, the Only Oracle of Man_ argued for deism, the belief that people should understand God through reason and nature rather than scripture. It is often called one of the first deist books published in America.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this author, better known as the leader of the Green Mountain Boys.

tossups.p: In 1770, after a New York court ruled against settlers who held land grants from New Hampshire governor Benning Wentworth, this man reportedly said, “The gods of the valleys are not the gods of the hills.” He then organized a militia to resist New York’s officials.
tossups.r: That militia, the Green Mountain Boys, later captured Fort Ticonderoga. For 10 points, name this founding father of Vermont.

tossups.p: New York officials called this man’s followers the “Bennington Mob,” and New York’s governor, William Tryon, offered a reward for his capture. His militia met at the Catamount Tavern in Bennington and drove out settlers who held land titles from New York.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this leader of the Green Mountain Boys who later captured Fort Ticonderoga.

tossups.p: During the Revolution, this man, his brother Ira, and other local leaders secretly negotiated with Frederick Haldimand, the British governor of Quebec, about their region possibly rejoining the British Empire. Critics accused him of treason, while supporters said he was only pressuring Congress to recognize that region.
tossups.r: That region, Vermont, became the 14th state in 1791. For 10 points, name this leader of the Green Mountain Boys.

tossups.p: This man and his youngest brother, Ira, bought up land along the Onion River through a family company, and Ira later founded the University of Vermont. Both brothers were leaders of the independent republic that became the state of Vermont.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this older brother, the leader of the Green Mountain Boys.

tossups.p: In July 1775, a meeting of local leaders chose Seth Warner instead of this man to command a new Continental regiment raised in the New Hampshire Grants. This man then joined the invasion of Canada as a volunteer and was captured outside Montreal that September.
tossups.r: Two months before that vote, he had captured Fort Ticonderoga. For 10 points, name this leader of the Green Mountain Boys.

tossups.p: Benedict Arnold arrived with a commission from Massachusetts and argued with this man over who should command their joint attack, but this man’s soldiers refused to follow anyone else. Afterward, Arnold sailed north and raided Fort St. Johns in Canada.
tossups.r: The two men had captured Fort Ticonderoga together. For 10 points, name this leader of the Green Mountain Boys.

tossups.p: Days after this man’s most famous victory, men under Seth Warner captured the nearby British post at Crown Point. The next winter, Henry Knox hauled cannons from the fort this man had taken all the way to Boston.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this leader of the Green Mountain Boys who captured Fort Ticonderoga.

tossups.p: An Amtrak train between New York City and Vermont and a well-known furniture company are both named for this man. He died in Burlington in 1789, two years before the state he helped create joined the Union.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Vermont hero who led the Green Mountain Boys in capturing Fort Ticonderoga.

tossups.p: Before moving north, this man was a part owner of an iron furnace in Salisbury, Connecticut, not far from his birthplace of Litchfield. In the land between New York and New Hampshire, he then led a militia that fought New York’s claim to that land.
tossups.r: That militia was the Green Mountain Boys. For 10 points, name this man who captured Fort Ticonderoga in 1775.

tossups.p: The fort this man captured in 1775 had been built by the French as Fort Carillon [“kah-ree-YOHN”]. Before dawn, he gathered his men at Hand’s Cove in what is now Vermont and crossed Lake Champlain in the few boats they could find.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this leader of the Green Mountain Boys who took Fort Ticonderoga.

tossups.p: A statue of this man stands at the entrance to the Vermont State House in Montpelier, and Vermont chose him as one of the two people it honors in the U.S. Capitol’s National Statuary Hall. A Navy submarine was also named for him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this leader of the Green Mountain Boys who seized Fort Ticonderoga in 1775.

trap.title: Allen, Arnold, or Warner?
trap.body: Three patriots appear in Fort Ticonderoga clues: Ethan Allen led the Green Mountain Boys, Benedict Arnold shared command with a commission from Massachusetts, and Seth Warner captured nearby Crown Point and later commanded the Green Mountain Boys’ Continental regiment. Ethan’s youngest brother, Ira Allen, was a founder of Vermont too, so “Allen” alone earns only a prompt. Some tossups also want the fort itself, not the man.
trap.fix: “Great Jehovah,” the capture near Montreal, the _Narrative_ of his captivity, and _Reason, the Only Oracle of Man_ mean Ethan Allen. The West Point treason plot means Arnold, and the University of Vermont means Ira. If the question asks for “this fort,” say “Fort Ticonderoga.”
